analysis.one_liner: Requires double-walled underground fuel tanks with leak monitoring near drinking water sources.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from March 2004 until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, with 5 cosponsors and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Underground storage tanks at gas stations and fuel sites can leak gasoline and MTBE, a fuel additive, into groundwater and drinking water wells. This bill would have required any new or replaced underground tank or pipe within 1,000 feet of a community water system, a drinking water well, or other sensitive area to be built with a second layer of containment — such as a double-walled tank — and monitored for leaks in the space between the layers. Violations would have carried civil penalties. It was introduced in March 2004 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who get their drinking water from community water systems or wells near underground fuel tanks would get a new layer of protection: tanks installed or replaced near those water sources would need a second wall of containment and constant leak monitoring, so leaks would be caught before gasoline or MTBE reached the water. States keep their authority to set stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households near fuel tanks and drinking water wells

how_it_helps.text: Any new or replaced underground fuel tank or piping within 1,000 feet of a community water system, a drinking water well, or other sensitive area would have to be secondarily contained — double-walled tanks and piping, dispenser liners, or tanks inside an impervious barrier — with the space between the two walls monitored for leaks.
Violations of the containment requirements would carry civil penalties, giving the existing enforcement framework a new tool.
The bill explicitly preserved the right of states to enforce stricter secondary containment rules than the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of underground fuel storage tanks — gas stations, fuel distributors, and other petroleum storage sites — would pay to install double-walled tanks, liners, sumps, and leak-monitoring equipment whenever they put in or replace a tank near a water source. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas stations and fuel storage tank operators

drawbacks.text: The requirements would raise costs for owners and operators of gas stations and other fuel storage sites, since double-walled tanks, piping sumps, dispenser liners, and leak monitoring are more expensive than single-walled systems.

The bill applied only to new or replaced tanks and piping. Existing single-walled tanks that were not dug up and replaced would not have to be secondarily contained, so much of the contamination risk from tanks already in the ground would have remained.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and durable: MTBE and petroleum leaks from underground tanks have poisoned wells and community water systems, and double-walled tanks with leak monitoring catch spills before they reach drinking water. The costs fall on tank owners — especially small independent gas stations, which would bear the expense of double-walled tanks and monitoring equipment — but only when they install or replace a tank, which they must do eventually anyway, and only within 1,000 feet of a water source. The honest objection to the design is its narrowness: it does nothing about the many existing single-walled tanks already in the ground, which is where a large share of contamination risk sits. On balance it was a modest, targeted public-health protection whose costs were manageable and whose benefits fell on people who drink the water.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, which never took it up, so it expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: John Dingell and four Democratic colleagues introduced H.R. 3940 on March 11, 2004.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on March 30, 2004, to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gas station owners and other fuel tank operators avoided the cost of installing double-walled tanks and leak-monitoring systems, and the communities near those tanks kept living with the existing contamination risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fuel tank operators who avoided compliance costs

for.name: John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring secondary containment of underground storage tanks near drinking water sources.

for.name: 5 of 205 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Hilda Solis, Lois Capps, Edward Markey, Albert Wynn, and the sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee and its environment subcommittee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and it was never brought to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill; but with no hearing, no vote, and no recorded opposition, there is no roll-call record showing where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Petroleum marketers and underground storage tank owners (gas stations, fuel terminals)
industries.note: They would have had to install double-walled tanks and piping with leak monitoring — more expensive than single-walled systems — whenever they put in or replaced a tank near a water source. Their cost of doing business is the public's gain of cleaner drinking water.

industries.industry: Underground storage tank and containment equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have created demand for double-walled tanks, liners, dispenser sumps, and leak-detection equipment among tank owners nationwide.

The bill targets the contamination end of the MTBE problem rather than its use. Stricter leak containment near water sources reduces the pathway by which MTBE and petroleum reach groundwater, without banning the additive itself.
